case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a relator in a False Claims Act qui tam suit who did not originally bring the action may voluntarily dismiss the case under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a) after the government has declined to intervene, and whether CMS's Medicare inpatient admission policies constituted 'substantive legal standards' requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primary: False Claims Act (FCA), 31 U.S.C. § 3730 (qui tam provisions governing voluntary dismissal); Secondary: 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2) (Medicare Act notice-and-comment requirement for 'substantive legal standards'); Administrative Procedure Act (APA) notice-and-comment rulemaking provisions
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Dr. Polansky, as relator, argues that a qui tam relator retains the authority to voluntarily dismiss a False Claims Act case under Rule 41(a) even after the government has declined to intervene, and that CMS's time-based Medicare inpatient admission policies (including the 24-hour benchmark standard conveyed through manual guidance without notice-and-comment rulemaking) constituted unlawful 'substantive legal standards' under the Medicare Act as interpreted by the Supreme Court in Allina Health Services v. Azar, thereby rendering false any claims submitted in reliance on those improperly promulgated standards.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Executive Health Resources and other respondents argue that the relator lacks independent authority to dismiss the FCA action after the government has declined to intervene, as the government retains a cognizable interest in the litigation that constrains unilateral relator action; additionally, respondents contend that CMS's Medicare inpatient admission guidance did not constitute 'substantive legal standards' requiring formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, and that any alleged procedural defects in the guidance do not give rise to FCA liability, with amici including the Chamber of Commerce, American Hospital Association, and American Health Care Association further arguing that imposing FCA liability based on compliance with longstanding agency guidance would create severe uncertainty for healthcare providers who reasonably relied on CMS manual instructions.

Allina Health Servs. v. Price, 863 F.3d 937 (D.C. Cir. 2017) - D.C. Circuit defined 'substantive legal standard' as a standard that 'creates, defines, and regulates the rights, duties, and powers of parties'

Wills v. Burwell, 306 F. Supp. 3d 684 (E.D. Pa. 2018) - District court consideration of 'substantive legal standard' definition predating Allina Supreme Court guidance
United States ex rel. Polansky v. Executive Health Resources, Inc., 17 F.4th 376 (3d Cir. 2021) - Third Circuit opinion below on certiorari review
United States ex rel. Polansky v. Executive Health Resources, Inc., 422 F. Supp. 3d 916 (E.D. Pa. 2019) - District court opinion addressing Medicare inpatient admission standards and FCA liability

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has achieved remarkable unanimity, and I am satisfied that the narrow procedural path Justice Gorsuch identified — that the relator's § 3730(b)(4)(B) right to 'conduct the action' incorporates Rule 41(a) dismissal authority, with the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) interest triggering Rule 41(a)(2) court oversight rather than unilateral dismissal — is both textually sound and institutionally appropriate. As I noted in my prior reasoning, Justice Alito's practical observation that the government here effectively consented to dismissal offers an even narrower ground: we can affirm the Third Circuit's result while correcting its doctrinal path, holding that § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement was satisfied on these facts without issuing a sweeping rule about relator authority in all circumstances. The strongest argument for Respondent — that § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement operates as a categorical bar rather than a procedural check — is adequately answered by Justice Barrett's textual observation that the provision says dismissal 'may be' obtained only with consent, which presupposes threshold relator authority to seek it. As Chief Justice, I will assign the opinion with instructions to write on the narrowest available ground — consent was given here, Rule 41(a)(2) court approval was the proper mechanism, and the Allina notice-and-comment question should be remanded rather than resolved broadly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The conference has reached a well-reasoned consensus, and deliberation has only strengthened my confidence in the petitioner's position. Justice Gorsuch's structural point — that the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) interests trigger Rule 41(a)(2) court-supervised dismissal rather than unilateral relator action under 41(a)(1) — is the most elegant textual resolution, and I adopt it as the proper framework: it honors § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement without converting it into a perpetual veto that would trap relators in unsustainable litigation. Justice Alito's practical-consent observation provides a narrower alternative ground that Chief Justice Roberts rightly notes could resolve this case without broad pronouncement, but I agree with Justice Gorsuch that establishing the correct doctrinal framework matters independently of the particular facts here — the rule of law requires clarity, not merely case-specific validation. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, the plain text of § 1395hh(a)(2) as interpreted through Allina remains dispositive: CMS's time-based benchmarks functioned as binding conditions of payment regardless of their informal label, and permitting agencies to circumvent mandatory rulemaking through manual guidance would render Congress's explicit procedural command a nullity — a result my originalist methodology cannot countenance.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkably coherent synthesis, and I find Justice Gorsuch's textual framework — that § 3730(b)(4)(B)'s grant of the right to 'conduct the action' incorporates Rule 41(a)'s dismissal mechanics, with the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) interest triggering Rule 41(a)(2) court oversight rather than unilateral dismissal — to be the most doctrinally precise resolution, though I maintain my practical-consent gloss as an alternative ground. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement is jurisdictional rather than merely procedural, which would mean the relator lacks threshold authority to seek dismissal absent formal government consent — but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, the text's structure ('may be dismissed only if') presupposes the relator has that threshold authority and then conditions its exercise, which is a procedural rather than jurisdictional framing. Chief Justice Roberts's preference for a narrow ruling that affirms on the consent-was-given facts while correcting the Third Circuit's reasoning is institutionally sound and avoids unnecessary pronouncements on relator authority in cases where the government has not effectively participated. On the Allina question, I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett that remand is appropriate given the 'substantive legal standards' analysis, though I would flag the reliance concerns Justice Kavanaugh raises as relevant to any good-faith defense analysis on remand.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkably coherent synthesis, and I find Justice Gorsuch's structural argument most persuasive from my pragmatic perspective: the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) interests are adequately protected through Rule 41(a)(2)'s court-approval requirement, which means we need not choose between trapping relators in unsustainable litigation and granting them unconstrained dismissal authority — the judicial oversight mechanism does the work. Justice Jackson's point about procedural fairness resonates deeply with me: a framework that denies relators any exit mechanism would systematically disadvantage the individual whistleblowers — often healthcare workers or contractors with limited resources — who are the FCA's primary enforcement engine against fraud on Medicare and Medicaid programs serving vulnerable populations. Chief Justice Roberts's preference for a narrow ruling that resolves this case on the consent-was-given facts is institutionally sound, but I would go slightly further than he suggests: we should establish the correct doctrinal framework — that § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement persists as a procedural check throughout litigation, satisfied here by the government's effective participation — rather than leaving lower courts without guidance on the recurring question of relator dismissal authority. The strongest respondent argument, that § 3730(b)(1) cannot be bootstrapped into a post-declination dismissal mechanism, is actually neutralized by our collective reading since we are not bootstrapping but rather recognizing that the consent requirement operates continuously as the statute's structural safeguard for the government's retained interest.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the bench, though I want to sharpen the textual analysis. Justice Thomas raises the partial assignment framework from Vermont Agency correctly, but I think Justice Gorsuch identifies the more precise mechanism: the relator's post-declination status as the party 'conducting the action' under § 3730(b)(4)(B) incorporates Rule 41(a)'s dismissal framework, with the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) interest triggering Rule 41(a)(2)'s court-approval requirement rather than unilateral dismissal under 41(a)(1). Justice Barrett's structural point about the 'dual-party character' of qui tam suits is well-taken — the government's interest doesn't dissolve upon declination, which is precisely why § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement operates as a procedural check rather than a categorical bar. The strongest counterargument — that the government's declination should be read as a complete divestiture of its procedural rights, leaving § 3730(b)(1) inapplicable — fails because it would create the anomaly of relators having unconstrained dismissal authority over claims brought nominally 'for the United States Government,' a result the statute's text and structure cannot support.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find broad agreement with my colleagues on the core textual question, though I want to sharpen the analysis. Justice Thomas correctly identifies that § 3730(b)(1)'s partial assignment framework from Vermont Agency vests the relator with independent procedural authority once the government declines, and I agree that reading § 3730(c)'s enumerated government controls as constraining a non-intervening relator would import restrictions the text does not plainly impose. Where I part slightly from Justice Alito's practical-consent approach is that I think the textual structure matters independently of whether the government happened to consent here — the rule of law requires we establish the correct framework, not merely validate the outcome. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, the plain text of § 1395hh(a)(2) and Allina's holding are dispositive: CMS cannot launder substantive legal standards through manual guidance to avoid the rulemaking requirements Congress mandated, and the reliance concerns Justice Kavanaugh raises, while sympathetic, cannot override a clear statutory command — providers who relied on improperly promulgated guidance did so at their own risk when the statute's requirements were publicly known.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference has reached a well-reasoned consensus, and I find Justice Gorsuch's structural argument particularly clarifying: the correct framework matters independently of whether the government happened to consent on these specific facts, because we are establishing a rule of law that will govern future cases. I remain persuaded that § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement operates as a persistent structural safeguard — not merely a filing-stage formality — and that Rule 41(a)(2) court-supervised dismissal with government consent is the proper procedural vehicle, which harmonizes the relator's right to 'conduct the action' under § 3730(b)(4)(B) with the government's retained financial and sovereign interests. Justice Thomas's textualist point that § 3730(c)'s enumerated controls may be intervention-specific retains some force, but I continue to think the stronger reading treats § 3730(b)(1) as a structural check that persists throughout litigation given that these suits are brought nominally 'in the name of the Government.' On the Allina question, I maintain my preference for Chief Justice Roberts's narrow approach — remanding rather than broadly resolving FCA liability for good-faith reliance on longstanding CMS manual guidance — because the reliance concerns for healthcare providers are substantial and the case can be resolved without reaching that question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The conference has converged on a textually sound framework, and I find Justice Gorsuch's structural argument most precisely captures the correct rule: § 3730(b)(4)(B)'s grant of the right to 'conduct the action' incorporates Rule 41(a)'s dismissal mechanisms, with the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) interest triggering Rule 41(a)(2) court-supervised dismissal rather than unilateral action under 41(a)(1). Chief Justice Roberts's preference for a narrow ruling — affirming on the consent-was-given facts rather than issuing a broad categorical rule — is institutionally prudent, but I think Justice Gorsuch is correct that establishing the proper doctrinal framework matters independently of the outcome here, because a rule that validates the result without clarifying the mechanism leaves lower courts without guidance on cases where the government does not effectively consent. The strongest counterargument for Respondent — that § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement is a perpetual categorical bar rather than a procedural check — fails on the text itself, which presupposes the relator has threshold authority to seek dismissal by conditioning it on consent rather than prohibiting it altogether. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan that Allina's 'substantive legal standards' framework is dispositive and that remand rather than outright rejection of FCA liability is the appropriate disposition.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The conference has converged on a textually and structurally sound framework, and I find Justice Gorsuch's precision about Rule 41(a)(2) particularly clarifying for my own analysis: the government's retained § 3730(c)(3) interest does not strip the relator of dismissal authority but instead channels that authority through court-supervised dismissal rather than unilateral action, which adequately protects the government's stake without creating the perverse trap of indefinite litigation. Justice Barrett's observation that § 3730(b)(1)'s 'may be dismissed only if' language presupposes threshold relator authority to seek dismissal is textually compelling and directly answers the respondent's strongest argument — that the consent requirement operates as a categorical bar rather than a procedural check. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that a framework denying relators any exit mechanism would undermine the FCA's private enforcement incentive structure, particularly for relators who lack resources to sustain prolonged litigation, and the Rule 41(a)(2) court-approval mechanism adequately addresses any concern about collusive or prejudicial dismissals. Chief Justice Roberts's preference for a narrow ruling resolving this case on the consent-was-given facts is institutionally prudent, but I agree with Justice Gorsuch that establishing the correct doctrinal framework matters independently of the particular outcome here.

John Roberts.reasoning: The statutory text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730 supports the relator's authority to seek voluntary dismissal under Rule 41(a), provided the government retains its consent role under § 3730(b)(1), which harmonizes the FCA's qui tam framework with Rule 41 without displacing either. The government's status as a real party in interest, as recognized in Eisenstein v. City of New York, 556 U.S. 928 (2009), means that any voluntary dismissal by the relator requires government consent, thereby protecting the government's cognizable interest while still permitting the relator to exercise dismissal rights — a narrow reading that preserves institutional balance. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), established that CMS policies setting substantive legal standards affecting provider rights require § 1395hh(a)(2) compliance, and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks, which effectively defined the boundary between reimbursable and non-reimbursable care, plausibly fall within that category. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would resolve the dismissal question on procedural grounds requiring government consent rather than broadly expanding or contracting relator authority, and remand the substantive FCA liability question for further proceedings under the Allina framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under a textualist and originalist reading of 31 U.S.C. § 3730, the FCA's qui tam provisions effect a 'partial assignment' of the government's claim to the relator, as recognized in Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000), vesting the relator with independent procedural rights including Rule 41(a) dismissal authority once the government has declined to intervene. The statutory text of § 3730(b)(1) authorizes the relator to bring and conduct the action, and § 3730(c)'s enumerated government controls apply specifically to circumstances where the government has intervened — reading those limitations to constrain a non-intervening relator's Rule 41(a) rights would require importing restrictions the text does not plainly impose. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, the plain text of 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2) requires notice-and-comment for 'substantive legal standards,' and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — which effectively determined provider reimbursement eligibility — functioned as binding standards creating legal obligations regardless of their informal label, consistent with Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019). Permitting agencies to circumvent mandatory rulemaking through manual guidance while still enforcing those standards as conditions of payment would undermine the structural separation between legislative rulemaking and mere interpretive guidance that Congress codified in § 1395hh(a)(2).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under a textualist reading of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1), the FCA explicitly requires both court and Attorney General consent for a relator to dismiss a qui tam action, and this consent requirement applies regardless of whether the government has formally intervened — the government's retained financial interest under § 3730(d) and its ability to intervene for good cause under § 3730(c)(3) constitute cognizable legal interests that cannot be extinguished by unilateral relator action under Rule 41(a). However, the practical resolution here favors Polansky because the government did in fact participate and effectively consented to dismissal, satisfying § 3730(b)(1)'s requirements even without formal intervention, meaning the Third Circuit's affirmance of dismissal was correct even if its reasoning was flawed. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks conveyed through manual guidance — which created binding operational standards that determined provider reimbursement eligibility — plausibly constitute 'substantive legal standards' under § 1395hh(a)(2) as interpreted in Allina Health Services v. Azar, though FCA liability predicated on compliance with longstanding agency guidance raises serious reliance concerns that counsel against expansive liability findings. The practical consequences for healthcare providers who reasonably relied on CMS manual instructions, as emphasized by the Chamber of Commerce and hospital association amici, weigh heavily against extending FCA liability in this context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1), a relator's dismissal authority requires court and Attorney General consent, but this provision governs the pre-declination posture; post-declination, the relator assumes primary control of the litigation and Rule 41(a) operates in conjunction with the FCA's structural framework, which under § 3730(c)(3) preserves the relator's 'status and rights' even when the government later seeks to intervene. The government's retained rights post-declination under § 3730(c)(3) are explicitly conditioned on not disturbing the relator's primary status, meaning those rights cannot be construed to strip the relator of the ability to manage and conclude litigation the relator is primarily conducting. As Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens recognized, the relator holds a partial assignment of the government's claim, and once the government declines intervention, the relator's control over that assigned interest must include the ability to voluntarily dismiss under Rule 41(a), subject to court approval and notice to the government as a safeguard for its residual interests. Pragmatically, denying relators this authority would trap them in litigation they can no longer sustain, undermining the FCA's purpose of incentivizing private enforcement against fraud on vulnerable public programs like Medicare.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 3730(b)(1) explicitly requires both court and Attorney General consent for dismissal of qui tam actions, and § 3730(c)(3) preserves the relator's 'right to conduct the action' after government declination — but critically, the government retains cognizable statutory interests that must be respected through proper procedural channels. The research confirms that when the government declines intervention, it must re-intervene under § 3730(c)(3) before seeking dismissal under § 3730(c)(2)(A), and once that procedural gateway is satisfied, Rule 41(a) governs the mechanics of dismissal. This reading harmonizes the FCA's structural design — which treats qui tam suits as brought 'in the name of the Government' — with Rule 41(a)'s workable framework, avoiding the anomaly of a relator having either no dismissal mechanism or an unconstrained one. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), makes clear that CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks, which effectively define the boundary between covered and non-covered care, constitute 'substantive legal standards' under § 1395hh(a)(2) requiring notice-and-comment, and FCA liability predicated on compliance with improperly promulgated guidance cannot be insulated merely because providers relied on those unlawful agency instructions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Reading the plain text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730, subsection (b)(1) expressly authorizes the relator to bring the action 'for the person and for the United States Government,' and subsection (b)(4)(B) confirms that when the government declines to intervene, the relator 'shall have the right to conduct the action.' Nothing in § 3730(c)(3) strips the relator of the procedural tools ordinarily available to a party conducting litigation, and the statute's silence on relator-initiated dismissal after government declination does not preclude Rule 41(a) — it incorporates it, because the relator steps into the role of the party prosecuting the case. The government retains a cognizable interest under § 3730(c)(3) that triggers court oversight under Rule 41(a)(2) rather than the unilateral right of dismissal under 41(a)(1), meaning the district court must approve dismissal on 'terms it considers proper,' which adequately protects the government's residual interest without denying the relator standing to seek dismissal altogether. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), makes clear that § 1395hh(a)(2) requires notice-and-comment for any policy that 'creates, defines, and regulates the rights, duties, and powers of parties,' and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — which determined whether hospitals would be reimbursed at all — plainly meet that standard regardless of how CMS chose to label the guidance.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1) explicitly requires both court and Attorney General consent for a relator to dismiss a qui tam action, but this restriction applies to the original filing stage; once the government has declined to intervene yet retains residual rights under § 3730(c)(3)—including the right to be served with pleadings and to intervene later upon showing good cause—the structural framework of the FCA contemplates that the relator, as the party prosecuting the action, retains Rule 41(a) dismissal authority subject to government consent requirements that attach through the government's continued cognizable interest. The government's partial assignment of its damages claim to the relator under Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000), does not extinguish the relator's procedural authority to manage litigation they are actively prosecuting; rather, the government's residual § 3730(c)(3) rights mean that Rule 41(a) dismissal requires government consent—which here the government provided—making the dismissal procedurally proper. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), establishes that CMS must comply with § 1395hh(a)(2) when promulgating substantive legal standards, and time-based inpatient admission benchmarks conveyed only through manual guidance that effectively determined provider reimbursement rights plausibly qualify as such standards, though the practical workability concerns raised by the hospital amici regarding retroactive FCA liability for good-faith reliance on longstanding agency guidance counsel judicial restraint in extending this theory.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A textualist reading of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1) reveals that the FCA's dismissal provision—requiring written consent of both the court and the Attorney General—operates as a constraint on dismissal that applies regardless of whether the government has formally intervened, meaning the relator retains standing as a 'party' to invoke Rule 41(a) subject to that consent requirement rather than being stripped of dismissal authority entirely upon government declination. The structural architecture of § 3730 confirms that the relator brings the action 'for the person and for the United States Government,' preserving a dual-party character that does not dissolve upon declination; the government's retained consent right under § 3730(b)(1) is best read as a check on relator authority, not a displacement of it. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), established that § 1395hh(a)(2) requires notice-and-comment for policies that establish 'substantive legal standards,' and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks—which effectively determined provider reimbursement eligibility and created binding operational criteria—fall within that definition as articulated by the D.C. Circuit in Allina Health Servs. v. Price, 863 F.3d 937 (D.C. Cir. 2017), making claims submitted under those improperly promulgated standards potentially actionable under the FCA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1) explicitly states that a qui tam action 'may be dismissed only if the court and the Attorney General give written consent,' which on its face applies to relator-initiated dismissals regardless of whether the government has intervened — meaning the government retains a cognizable interest sufficient to require its consent, but that consent requirement does not strip the relator of the threshold authority to seek dismissal under Rule 41(a). The structural logic of the FCA supports Polansky's position: the government's declination of intervention does not extinguish its legal interest in the litigation (as Vermont Agency confirms the relator holds only a partial assignment of the government's injury), but the consent requirement of § 3730(b)(1) operates as a procedural check on dismissal rather than a categorical bar to relator-initiated voluntary dismissal motions. On the Medicare notice-and-comment question, Allina Health Services v. Azar, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), establishes that CMS must comply with § 1395hh(a)(2) when promulgating 'substantive legal standards,' and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — which effectively defined the boundary between reimbursable and non-reimbursable care — functionally created binding obligations on providers, satisfying the D.C. Circuit's definition of standards that 'create, define, and regulate the rights, duties, and powers of parties,' even if conveyed through manual guidance rather than formal rulemaking.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a relator in a False Claims Act qui tam suit who did not originally bring the action can voluntarily dismiss the case under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a), and whether CMS's Medicare inpatient admission policies constituted 'substantive legal standards' requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2).

case_analysis.petitioner_position: Dr. Polansky, as relator, argues that he retains the right to voluntarily dismiss the FCA qui tam action under Rule 41(a) even after the government declined to intervene, and that CMS's time-based inpatient admission policies (including the 24-hour benchmark conveyed through manual guidance without notice-and-comment rulemaking) constituted 'substantive legal standards' under the Medicare Act that were procedurally invalid under Allina, thereby undermining the False Claims Act liability predicated on those standards.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Executive Health Resources and other respondents argue that the relator lacks independent authority to dismiss the action under Rule 41(a) once the government has appeared in the litigation, and that CMS's manual guidance on inpatient admission criteria did not rise to the level of 'substantive legal standards' requiring formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, making the underlying FCA claims legally deficient because no valid enforceable standard was violated.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and the textual arguments have genuinely moved me. As I noted in my prior reasoning, Justice Gorsuch's invocation of § 3730(c)(3)'s explicit preservation of 'the status and rights of the person initiating the action' is a textual argument I cannot dismiss under my own methodology — Congress demonstrated it knew how to subordinate relator rights when it chose to, as in § 3730(c)(2)(A), and its deliberate choice not to do so in § 3730(c)(3) is textually significant. Justice Kagan's framing of the coherent statutory structure — the relator retains the mechanical ability to invoke Rule 41(a) while the government retains veto power through § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement — gives full operative effect to both provisions without surplusage, which satisfies my preference for narrow, text-grounded reasoning. As the opinion-assigning Justice, I would write narrowly to hold only that § 3730(c)(3) preserves relator Rule 41(a) authority subject to the § 3730(b)(1) consent requirement, and I would cabin the Allina holding to the specific procedural defect in CMS's admission benchmarks rather than broadly destabilizing Medicare's administrative framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable textual consensus, and I find the convergence of my colleagues' analysis on § 3730(c)(3) fully consistent with my originalist and textualist methodology. Justice Gorsuch's observation — which I noted in my prior reasoning — that Congress used precise limiting language in § 3730(c)(2) when it wished to constrain relator authority, while § 3730(c)(3) explicitly preserves 'the status and rights of the person initiating the action,' is textually dispositive under the original public meaning of the FCA's qui tam provisions. Chief Justice Roberts's shift is particularly significant: his acknowledgment that § 3730(c)(2)(A)'s 'notwithstanding the objections of the relator' language actually demonstrates Congress knew how to subordinate relator rights and chose not to do so in § 3730(c)(3) is precisely the kind of structural textual inference I find most persuasive. On the Allina question, my longstanding skepticism of agencies circumventing statutory procedural requirements — as expressed in my Azar v. Allina concurrence — reinforces that CMS's time-based admission benchmarks, which carried binding enforcement consequences, constituted 'substantive legal standards' requiring notice-and-comment under § 1395hh(a)(2), and predicating FCA liability on procedurally defective guidance is incompatible with the rule of law.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's textual observation about § 3730(c)(3)'s explicit preservation of 'the status and rights of the person initiating the action' remains the most compelling argument in this deliberation, and the near-unanimous convergence of my colleagues on this reading — including Chief Justice Roberts's shift — confirms that the textual case is strong enough that my prior structural concerns cannot override it. As a committed textualist, I must follow Congress's plain language even when the practical consequences complicate government litigation control, and § 3730(c)(3)'s limiting clause directly forecloses the inference that late government intervention extinguishes relator procedural rights. Justice Roberts correctly notes that § 3730(c)(2)(A)'s 'notwithstanding the objections of the relator' language actually demonstrates Congress knew how to subordinate relator rights when it chose to, making the absence of such language in § 3730(c)(3) textually significant rather than merely an argument from silence. On the Allina question, the rule-of-law concerns about predicating FCA liability — with its treble damages — on guidance that was never validly promulgated through notice-and-comment are substantial and consistent with my longstanding skepticism of agencies circumventing statutory procedural requirements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The convergence of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum on the textual significance of § 3730(c)(3)'s explicit preservation of 'the status and rights of the person initiating the action' — as Justice Gorsuch, Justice Barrett, and Justice Kagan each independently identify — reinforces my confidence that this is the correct reading. Chief Justice Roberts's shift to the petitioner's position is particularly meaningful because he was the most serious voice for the respondent's structural argument, and his acknowledgment that § 3730(c)(2)(A)'s 'notwithstanding the objections of the relator' language actually demonstrates Congress knew how to subordinate relator rights when it chose to — and did not do so in § 3730(c)(3) — effectively dismantles the strongest counterargument. From my pragmatic perspective, I would emphasize in any opinion I join or write that the real-world consequences for whistleblowers matter: stripping relators of Rule 41(a) authority would trap them in litigation indefinitely, chilling the private enforcement mechanism Congress deliberately created. On the Allina question, Justice Jackson's point about fair notice resonates deeply with me — imposing treble FCA damages on standards never validly promulgated through notice-and-comment is precisely the kind of procedural unfairness that undermines both the rule of law and the rights of defendants who lacked meaningful opportunity to challenge the underlying standards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable textual convergence, and I find the collective analysis reinforces rather than undermines my position. Justice Roberts's shift is particularly significant — his acknowledgment that § 3730(c)(3)'s explicit preservation language 'without limiting the status and rights of the person initiating the action' directly undermines his own prior structural argument about government primacy confirms that the textual evidence here is genuinely decisive. The harmonization I've advocated throughout — relator retains Rule 41(a) dismissal authority while government retains veto power through § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement — gives full operative effect to every relevant provision without rendering any surplusage, which is precisely the kind of coherent statutory reading my pragmatic textualist methodology demands. On Allina, Justice Jackson correctly identifies that the destabilization concern cuts toward requiring notice-and-comment, not away from it, because Congress enacted § 1395hh(a)(2) specifically to prevent agencies from imposing binding substantive standards through informal guidance that circumvents procedural protections — and CMS's time-based admission benchmarks with real FCA enforcement consequences fit that profile exactly.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable textual consensus, and I find the collective engagement with § 3730(c)(3)'s 'without limiting the status and rights of the person initiating the action' language fully vindicates the textualist methodology I applied in round one. Chief Justice Roberts's shift is particularly significant — his acknowledgment that § 3730(c)(2)(A)'s 'notwithstanding the objections of the relator' language actually demonstrates Congress knew how to subordinate relator rights when it chose to, and conspicuously declined to do so in § 3730(c)(3), is exactly the kind of negative-implication canon that textualism demands we apply. Justice Alito's partial concession is also telling: even a justice skeptical of broad relator authority concedes that § 3730(c)(3)'s plain text cannot be read away, which confirms that the government's Article II interests — while real — must be vindicated through the consent mechanism Congress actually provided in § 3730(b)(1), not through judicial inference that silently extinguishes relator procedural standing. On the Allina question, I remain convinced that predicating FCA liability — with its treble damages and qui tam enforcement incentives — on CMS guidance that never underwent notice-and-comment review under § 1395hh(a)(2) raises both statutory and rule-of-law concerns that cannot be dismissed as mere administrative inconvenience.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable convergence, and the textual analysis has only strengthened through deliberation. Chief Justice Roberts's shift is particularly significant — his acknowledgment that § 3730(c)(3)'s explicit preservation of 'the status and rights of the person initiating the action' directly undermines his own prior structural inference confirms that this is the textually decisive provision. As I noted in my prior reasoning, Congress demonstrated it knew how to subordinate relator rights when it chose to (§ 3730(c)(2)), and its deliberate choice not to do so in § 3730(c)(3) cannot be read away through structural inference. I would write separately to emphasize, consistent with Roberts's minimalist instinct, that today's holding is narrow: the relator retains Rule 41(a) dismissal authority, but the government's consent requirement under § 3730(b)(1) remains a meaningful and constitutionally significant check that preserves the government's Article II litigation interests — this framing addresses Justice Alito's lingering concerns about executive authority while honoring the statutory text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The deliberation has substantially reinforced my position. Justice Gorsuch's textual observation about § 3730(c)(3)'s explicit preservation of relator rights 'without limiting the status and rights of the person initiating the action' remains the most decisive textual signal, and I note that even Chief Justice Roberts — whose structural argument about § 3730(c)(2)(A) presented the most serious challenge — has now acknowledged that this provision actually demonstrates Congress knew how to subordinate relator rights when it chose to, and elected not to do so in § 3730(c)(3). The coherent reading that gives full operative effect to both § 3730(b)(1)'s consent requirement and § 3730(c)(3)'s preservation clause — the relator retains the mechanical ability to move for dismissal while the government retains veto power through consent — avoids surplusage and honors the statutory structure Congress deliberately constructed. On the Allina question, the near-unanimous view that CMS's time-based admission benchmarks constitute 'substantive legal standards' under § 1395hh(a)(2) is well-grounded, and predicating FCA liability with its treble damages on guidance that was never validly promulgated through notice-and-comment raises the precise rule-of-law concerns that both the Medicare Act's procedural requirements and my textualist methodology are designed to prevent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The convergence across all nine justices on the § 3730(c)(3) textual argument — which Justice Gorsuch identified and which even Chief Justice Roberts now acknowledges he cannot dismiss — reinforces my confidence that the relator retains Rule 41(a) dismissal authority subject to government consent. Roberts's shift is particularly significant: his structural argument that § 3730(c)(2)(A) signals government primacy was the strongest counterargument, and his recognition that this provision actually demonstrates Congress knew how to subordinate relator rights when it wanted to — and chose not to in § 3730(c)(3) — eliminates the most serious textual obstacle to the petitioner's position. On the Allina question, my background as a public defender makes me especially attentive to the fair notice problem Justice Thomas identifies: imposing treble FCA damages based on CMS guidance that was never validly promulgated through notice-and-comment is precisely the kind of procedural unfairness that § 1395hh(a)(2) was designed to prevent, and the practical enforcement consequences of CMS's time-based benchmarks confirm they functioned as substantive legal standards regardless of their informal label. I write separately to emphasize that today's ruling should be read narrowly — the government's consent requirement under § 3730(b)(1) remains a meaningful structural check on relator dismissal authority, and courts should scrutinize whether that consent was properly obtained.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FCA's carefully calibrated framework under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b) and (c) reflects Congress's deliberate allocation of authority between the government and relators, and when the government intervenes — even belatedly under § 3730(c)(3) — it acquires the full suite of litigation rights including the ability to seek dismissal under Rule 41(a) as the real party in interest. The structural logic of the statute supports reading the government's later intervention as restoring its primary litigating authority, since § 3730(c)(2)(A) already contemplates government dismissal authority 'notwithstanding the objections of the relator,' suggesting Congress did not intend relators to hold an absolute veto over dismissal once the government is an active participant. On the Allina question, applying Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), narrowly and consistent with minimalist principles, CMS's manual guidance on inpatient admission criteria — while influential — did not rise to the level of a 'substantive legal standard' within the meaning of § 1395hh(a)(2) because it lacked the binding legal effect necessary to trigger notice-and-comment obligations, and extending Allina broadly here would destabilize Medicare's administrative framework in ways Congress did not clearly authorize. The institutional legitimacy concerns counsel against expansive readings of either provision that would invite relators to weaponize procedural rules against the government's considered litigation judgments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730 must be read according to its plain meaning and original public understanding. Section 3730(b)(1) permits a relator to bring an action 'for the person and for the United States Government,' and § 3730(c)(3) expressly permits the government to intervene at a later stage 'upon a showing of good cause,' which necessarily implies that once the government intervenes, the procedural mechanisms of Rule 41(a) become available to the government as a party — and by extension, the relator retains standing as the original party-plaintiff to invoke Rule 41(a) dismissal subject to the court's and government's consent, consistent with the statute's structural framework. On the Medicare Act question, Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), which I joined, firmly established that CMS's manual guidance setting time-based inpatient admission benchmarks without notice-and-comment rulemaking violated 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2) when those policies constituted 'substantive legal standards,' and FCA liability predicated on procedurally invalid agency guidance raises serious concerns about imposing liability based on standards that lacked the force of law. The original meaning of the FCA's qui tam provisions, read alongside Rule 41(a)'s text, supports the relator's authority to seek dismissal while the government retains consent rights as an intervening party, preserving the structural balance Congress intended.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I read 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b) and (c) carefully: the FCA establishes a specific statutory framework governing dismissal of qui tam actions that operates as lex specialis relative to Rule 41(a)'s general provisions. The government's dismissal authority under § 3730(c)(2)(A) operates independently of formal intervention status, as the statutory text does not condition that authority on prior intervention during the seal period — the government retains supervisory interests in FCA litigation regardless of its initial election. On the Allina/notice-and-comment question, while I take seriously the Medicare Act's § 1395hh(a)(2) requirement for notice-and-comment rulemaking for 'substantive legal standards,' CMS's manual guidance on inpatient admission criteria, including the 24-hour benchmark, functioned as interpretive guidance rather than binding substantive standards creating new legal obligations, and predicating FCA liability on procedurally defective standards would raise serious practical concerns for healthcare enforcement that Congress did not intend. The Third Circuit correctly affirmed dismissal, and the government's practical interest in controlling litigation brought nominally in its name — consistent with the executive's Article II supervisory role — supports affirming the judgment below.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1), the government's consent is required before a relator may dismiss a qui tam action, but this provision equally contemplates that the relator — as a partial assignee of the government's claim per Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000) — retains independent procedural standing to invoke Rule 41(a) once the government has appeared in the litigation, because the government's later intervention under § 3730(c)(3) does not extinguish the relator's original party status. The practical reality is that denying relators like Dr. Polansky the ability to seek voluntary dismissal would leave them trapped in litigation they initiated, unable to respond to changed circumstances, which undermines the FCA's purpose of incentivizing private enforcement on behalf of the public fisc. On the Allina question, CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — including the 24-hour guidance disseminated through manual updates — functionally operated as binding substantive legal standards affecting Medicare payment determinations, and under Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), such standards require notice-and-comment rulemaking under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2), meaning FCA liability predicated on those procedurally defective standards is legally infirm. The vulnerable Medicare beneficiaries and healthcare providers subject to these admission criteria deserve the procedural protections Congress mandated, and allowing enforcement through the FCA of standards that were never validly promulgated would permit the government to circumvent the very safeguards designed to ensure fair and transparent rulemaking.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1) requires government consent before a relator may voluntarily dismiss, but this consent requirement presupposes the relator retains the underlying authority to move for dismissal under Rule 41(a) — the FCA channels and conditions that authority rather than extinguishing it. When the government declines to intervene initially but later appears under § 3730(c)(3), the relator does not lose the procedural standing as the party who initiated and has been prosecuting the action; the government's late appearance supplements rather than supplants the relator's role. The statutory structure of § 3730(c)(1)-(3) preserves the relator's rights 'subject to limitations,' which means the relator retains Rule 41(a) dismissal authority subject to the government's consent under § 3730(b)(1) — a reading that gives coherent effect to both provisions without rendering either surplusage. On the Allina question, CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks conveyed through manual guidance functioned as operative legal standards affecting provider reimbursement in a manner that Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), would require to go through notice-and-comment rulemaking under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2), and FCA liability predicated on violations of procedurally invalid standards raises serious workability concerns that counsel against affirmance.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1) expressly preserves the relator's right to dismiss subject to government consent, and § 3730(c)(3) explicitly states that late government intervention occurs 'without limiting the status and rights of the person initiating the action' — textual signals that Congress intended relators to retain meaningful procedural authority including Rule 41(a) dismissal rights, provided the government has an opportunity to object. The FCA's carefully calibrated scheme allocates party control at each stage through specific statutory provisions rather than displacing general procedural rules wholesale, and where Congress wanted to limit relator authority it did so expressly, as in § 3730(c)(2). On the Allina question, Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), establishes that CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — conveyed through manual guidance affecting beneficiary entitlements — constitute 'substantive legal standards' under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2) requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking, and FCA liability predicated on violations of procedurally invalid agency guidance raises serious rule-of-law concerns that counsel in favor of the relator's position that the underlying standards were defective. Reading the statute's text and structure together, the relator here retains the right to invoke Rule 41(a) subject to the government's consent rights under § 3730(b)(1), and the procedurally defective CMS guidance cannot serve as the predicate for FCA liability without undermining the notice-and-comment requirements Congress mandated.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FCA's statutory structure under 31 U.S.C. § 3730 contemplates that a relator who initiates a qui tam action retains meaningful procedural rights throughout the litigation, including the ability to seek voluntary dismissal under Rule 41(a) with appropriate government consent mechanisms already built into § 3730(b)(1). The government's initial declination to intervene does not extinguish the relator's standing as the party who brought the action, and when the government later participates without formally intervening under § 3730(c)(3), the relator's foundational procedural rights as the initiating plaintiff should not be subordinated entirely to the government's litigation preferences. Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000), recognized the relator's partial assignment of the government's claim as conferring genuine Article III standing, which logically carries with it the procedural incidents of plaintiff status, including Rule 41(a) dismissal authority subject to the consent requirements Congress already specified. On the Allina question, CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks conveyed through manual guidance without notice-and-comment rulemaking bear the hallmarks of 'substantive legal standards' under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2) as interpreted in Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), and predicating FCA liability on procedurally defective standards raises serious concerns about fair notice and institutional legitimacy that counsel in favor of the petitioner's position.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textual analysis of 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(1) establishes that qui tam suits are brought 'in the name of the Government,' and the FCA's consent provisions contemplate that dismissal requires both court and Attorney General approval regardless of formal intervention status — this structure supports the relator retaining procedural standing to invoke Rule 41(a) as the nominal plaintiff while the government retains veto authority through the consent requirement. The FCA's architecture in § 3730(c) demonstrates that Congress carefully calibrated the government's retained authority even after declining to intervene, and reading Rule 41(a) in harmony with these provisions means a relator who originally filed the action retains the mechanical ability to move for voluntary dismissal, subject to the government's consent under § 3730(b)(1). On the Allina question, Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), established that CMS policies establishing 'substantive legal standards' affecting beneficiary entitlements require notice-and-comment rulemaking under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2), and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — including the 24-hour guidance — functionally operated as binding standards governing Medicare reimbursement eligibility, satisfying Allina's threshold, which would undermine the FCA liability predicated on those procedurally defective standards. The methodological consistency demanded by textualism requires giving full effect to both the FCA's consent framework and the Medicare Act's rulemaking mandate rather than permitting agencies to circumvent notice-and-comment through informal manual guidance that carries practical binding force.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As a relator who received a partial assignment of the government's damages claim under Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000), Dr. Polansky retains a cognizable interest in the litigation sufficient to invoke Rule 41(a), particularly where the government has appeared and can exercise its own oversight role — the statutory framework of 31 U.S.C. § 3730 contemplates relator agency even post-government appearance, and reading Rule 41(a) to categorically strip relators of dismissal authority would create procedural inequities inconsistent with the FCA's structural design. On the Medicare Act question, Azar v. Allina Health Services, 139 S. Ct. 1804 (2019), established that CMS policies affecting 'substantive legal standards' for Medicare payment require notice-and-comment rulemaking under 42 U.S.C. § 1395hh(a)(2), and CMS's time-based inpatient admission benchmarks — which functionally determined Medicare reimbursement eligibility and carried real enforcement consequences — bear the hallmarks of substantive standards rather than mere interpretive guidance. From a practical consequences standpoint, permitting agencies to impose binding admission criteria through manual guidance without notice-and-comment would undermine both the procedural fairness interests of healthcare providers and the structural accountability Congress mandated in § 1395hh(a)(2). The convergence of these two issues favors the petitioner, as the FCA claims predicated on procedurally invalid standards raise serious concerns about fair notice and due process that my background as a public defender makes me particularly attentive to.
